title: Infra engineering consolidated playbook: GPU fleet, cloud accounts, IaC modules, CI/CD, runbooks
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Overview

This consolidated playbook documents standard practices, ownership, and runbooks for Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering focused on GPU fleet & capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build, and core runbooks used by oncall. It is intended as the single source of truth for infra engineers and SREs.

Key goals:
- Ensure safe, repeatable changes to infra via IaC.
- Maintain predictable GPU capacity and graceful degradation.
- Standardize CI/CD pipelines and artifact promotion.
- Provide clear runbooks for common operational events.

Owners & teams

- Infra Platform (owner): infra-platform@redwood.ai
- GPU Fleet (owner): gpu-fleet@redwood.ai
- Cloud Accounts & Networking: cloud-accounts@redwood.ai
- CI/CD & Build: infra-ci@redwood.ai
- Oncall escalation: oncall-ops@redwood.ai

Each service below lists primary owner, backup, and escalation path.

1) GPU fleet & capacity planning

Purpose: run and scale GPU-backed inference pools for Redwood Dedicated and Private offerings while meeting latency SLOs and cost targets.

Services and components:
- gpu-fleet-manager: orchestration layer for node pools, autoscaler hooks.
- kv-cache-store: prefix cache used by model-serving to reduce tokens.
- node-provisioner: Terraform modules + boot images for GPU instances.

SLOs and alerting (production):
- P99 inference tail latency (single-token, p99): <= 400ms for hosted tier; <= 300ms for dedicated tier.
- Capacity headroom: >= 25% spare GPU capacity during peak 95th percentile traffic.
- Node provisioning time: new node ready and registered within 8 minutes.

Key metrics to track:
- gpu_utilization (per-pool), pod_ready_count, node_provision_time, queue_latency, eviction_rate.

Autoscaling and policies:
- Continuous batching tuned per model family.
- Horizontal scale: preferred. Use vertical scale only for special large-memory models.
- Burst pool: pre-warmed spot-backed nodes with fallback to on-demand under capacity crunch.

Capacity planning cadence:
1. Weekly usage review: owners review 7/30/90 day trends.
2. Monthly forecast: propose capacity commit changes.
3. Quarterly load test and canary: run synthetic peak at 1.3x expected peak.

Capacity table (example target pool sizes):
| Pool | Target GPUs | Headroom target | Instance type | Notes |
|------|-------------:|----------------:|---------------|-------|
| hosted-small | 64 | 30% | a10g | low-latency models |
| dedicated-general | 128 | 20% | a100-80g | reserved customer pools |
| burst-spot | 48 | 0% | g5 | spot-backed, pre-warmed |

Runbook: GPU out-of-capacity (brief)

Trigger: "gpu_pool_available_gpus < headroom_threshold" OR sustained queue_latency > 200ms for 5m.

Steps:
1. Pager: oncall receives alert (pagerduty gpu-fleet shortage).
2. Confirm: check dashboard (gpu-fleet-manager -> pool view), verify metric windows (5m, 15m).
3. Quick mitigations (5-15 minutes):
   - Increase autoscaler max for affected pool (infra-ci pipeline: promote autoscaler-config).
   - Enable burst pool: set burst_pool_enabled=true in runtime toggle service.
   - If autoscaler stuck, trigger manual node create via node-provisioner UI or run:
     ```bash
     infractl node provision --pool=<pool> --count=4 --type=a100-80g
     ```
4. Medium-term (30-120 minutes):
   - Migrate non-critical jobs to burst-spot.
   - Temporarily lower batch size for latency-sensitive routes using config overrides.
5. Post-incident: create incident summary, update capacity forecast, add lessons.

2) Cloud accounts & networking

Account structure and naming conventions:
- Accounts are organized by environment: core-prod, core-stage, core-dev, customer-<org>-prod.
- Projects/Accounts must include tags: owner, cost-center, environment, region.

Networking fundamentals:
- VPC-per-environment with standardized subnets (public/private): 10.<env>.<zone>.0/24 scheme.
- Shared services VPC (logging, observability, artifact registry) peered via transit gateway.
- Default security posture: deny-by-default with least-privilege security groups and network ACLs.

Private deployment considerations:
- For customer VPC integration, use dedicated VPC connectors and IP allowlists.
- Documented onboarding checklist: IP ranges, BGP/peering config, KMS key IDs, SLA requirements.

Network configuration reference (example):
| Item | Value | Owner | Notes |
|------|-------|-------|-------|
| Transit gateway | tgw-01 | cloud-accounts | used for cross-region peering |
| Observability VPC CIDR | 10.200.0.0/16 | infra-platform | central logging/metrics |

3) Terraform / IaC modules and patterns

Principles:
- Keep modules small and composable. Each module must have README, inputs, outputs, and example.
- All changes must go through CI and PR review; sensitive changes require an approver from security or cloud-accounts.
- Modules published to internal registry: registry.redwood.local/terraform.

Core modules:
- terraform-modules/networking: vpc, subnets, route-tables, nat, transit-gateway attachments.
- terraform-modules/gpu-node: instance profile, boot disk image, gpu device plugin, spot/ondemand options.
- terraform-modules/iam: least-privilege roles for each service.
- terraform-modules/k8s-cluster: EKS/GKE bootstrap, addon integration, nodegroup definitions.

Module example usage (snippet):
```hcl
module "gpu_nodes" {
  source = "registry.redwood.local/terraform-modules/gpu-node"
  name = "dedicated-general"
  instance_type = "a100-80g"
  desired_count = 128
  tags = { owner = "gpu-team" environment = "prod" }
}
```

Best-practices checklist for PRs:
1. Run terraform fmt and validate.
2. Run plan in CI with current state pull.
3. Annotate plan with risk tags (infrastructure-impact: low/medium/high).
4. Require 2 approvers for high-risk changes.
5. If state or backend changes are included, schedule a maintenance window.

State management:
- Remote state stored in central bucket with state-locking (DynamoDB/locks).
- Secrets must not be committed; use secret manager.

4) CI/CD and build systems

Pipelines and conventions:
- infra-ci: primary CI for Terraform and infra repos (GitHub Actions + self-hosted runners).
- infra-build: builds base AMIs, container images, and publishes to internal registries.
- Naming: pipelines follow repo-name/branch/action (e.g., infra/terraform-modules:main/plan).

Promotion flow:
1. PR branch -> plan job (automated).
2. Merge to main -> apply job gated by environment tag.
3. Canary deployments for infra changes affecting prod: apply to stage, validate, apply to prod during maintenance window.

Sample GitHub Actions job for Terraform plan:
```yaml
name: Terraform Plan
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, terraform]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="bucket=infra-terraform-state"
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
      - name: Upload Plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan
```

Build artifacts and registries:
- Container registry: registry.redwood.internal (images tagged by commit-sha + semver).
- AMI pipeline: packer builds validated images with included gpu drivers and NVidia toolkit.

5) Runbooks (operational playbooks)

This section contains high-level and step-by-step runbooks used by oncall. Keep runbooks concise; link to extended docs for context.

Runbook list (high-priority):
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook (detailed): link /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- infra-ci-failure: how to triage stuck Terraform applies and race conditions.
- network-outage: steps for investigating inter-region peering failures.

Incident triage template (confluence-style):
1. Summary (one-line).
2. Impact (services, customers, scale).
3. Timeline (ordered events).
4. Mitigation steps taken.
5. Root cause analysis.
6. Action items and owner assignments.

6) Infra team wiki conventions and templates

Page types and tags:
- architecture-overview, runbook, playbook, onboarding, cookbook.
- Use labels: team:<team-name>, infra-area:<area>, skl:runbook.

Template header (required fields):
- Title
- Summary (brief)
- Owner (team or person)
- Last Updated
- Related Pages
- Contact / Slack channel

Onboarding checklist for new infra hires:
- Access: GitHub, registry, cloud accounts, pagerduty.
- Hands-on tasks: run terraform plan against a non-prod module, deploy a test node via infractl, execute the GPU capacity simulation test.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets

- Provision node (infractl):
  infractl node provision --pool hosted-small --count 2 --type a10g

- Check pool utilization (prometheus):
  curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=gpu_utilization%7Bpool%3D%22hosted-small%22%7D"

- Rebuild AMI (packer):
  ./build-ami.sh --image-type gpu-base --output=ami-20250210

Glossary (short):
- Pool: logical grouping of GPU instances.
- Burst pool: pre-warmed spot-backed capacity used for short bursts.
- Node-provisioner: service that creates nodes via IaC when autoscaler needs more capacity.
